Wig out
WIG OWT
verb (Silent Generation slang)
Jazz and beat slang of the 1950s, built on wig as slang for the head or mind (to flip one’s wig, to go crazy, is of the same family). Wig itself is short for periwig, the false hair of earlier centuries. To wig out was to lose control — to go wild with excitement or to go to pieces — and the phrase passed from the jazz clubs to the teenagers and on into the 1960s.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

When a jazzman of 1957 said the crowd wigged out, he meant they went wild; when a mother said she was about to wig out, she meant the children had pushed her to the edge. Either way, the word means losing hold of the mind. Scripture prizes the opposite: "For God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind" (2Ti 1:7). Self-command is a kind of strength: "He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city" (Pro 16:32), while the man who flies apart "is like a city that is broken down, and without walls" (Pro 25:28). There is real comfort here, because sometimes a person wigs out not from temper but from fear and strain, and God does not scold such a one so much as steady him: "Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee" (Isa 26:3). The Gospels show the sharpest picture of all. A man so tormented by devils that no chain could hold him met Jesus, and afterward the townsfolk found him "sitting, and clothed, and in his right mind" (Mar 5:15). That is what Christ does for the wigged-out soul. A grandfather can tell the children: when you feel yourself coming apart, stop, pray, and fix your mind on the Lord who calms storms.

Webster 1828 Definition

Silent Generation slang (jazz and beat talk, 1950s; from wig, the head or mind) for losing control — answered by the sound mind God gives (2Ti 1:7) and the tormented man Christ left sitting in his right mind (Mar 5:15).

expand to see more

WIG OUT, v.i. (Silent Generation slang, 1950s; jazz and beat talk) To lose control; to go wild with excitement, or to go to pieces. "When the band hit that last chorus, the whole room wigged out."

Webster (1828) — WIG, noun 1. A covering for the head, consisting of hair interwoven or united by a kind of network; formerly much worn by men.

Decode for families: to wig out is to lose your head — and the 1828 wig was a covering of false hair, the very thing that flies off when you flip.

Key Scripture

2Ti 1:7 — "For God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind."

Pro 16:32 — "He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city."

Pro 25:28 — "He that hath no rule over his own spirit is like a city that is broken down, and without walls."

Isa 26:3 — "Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee: because he trusteth in thee."

Mar 5:15 — "And they come to Jesus, and see him that was possessed with the devil, and had the legion, sitting, and clothed, and in his right mind: and they were afraid."

Modern Corruption

A lively word that can mean harmless excitement, but it can also make losing control sound fun or excusable, when Scripture calls us to a sound mind.

expand to see more

When wig out means only that the crowd went wild at a ballgame, it is harmless. Joy can be loud. And when a tired mother says she is about to wig out, she is confessing weakness, not boasting of it, and she deserves help more than a lecture.

The caution is that the jazz world of the 1950s sometimes used the word for the effects of drink and drugs, and the counterculture after it made wigging out a goal. Scripture never treats losing one’s mind as freedom. Rage, panic, and intoxication are things to be ruled, not sought (Pro 25:28). The Christian aims for the sound mind and the perfect peace God promises.
